events/canossa-1077/summary: Excommunicated by Pope Gregory VII for appointing bishops, Emperor Henry IV stood penitent in the snow outside Canossa castle for three days to obtain absolution. The Investiture Controversy, settled by the Concordat of Worms (1122), established the church's independence in appointing clergy.
events/canossa-1077/causes/0: Gregorian reform against lay investiture and simony
events/canossa-1077/consequences/1: Distinction of spiritual and temporal power in the West
events/first-crusade-1096/summary: Responding to Byzantine appeals and Pope Urban II's call at Clermont (1095), armies of Western knights and pilgrims marched east, massacring Rhineland Jews on the way and capturing Jerusalem in July 1099 with great slaughter. Crusader states were founded in the Levant.
events/first-crusade-1096/causes/1: Urban II's preaching and penitential indulgence
events/anselm-cur-deus-homo-1098/summary: Archbishop Anselm of Canterbury, in exile, completed Why God Became Man, arguing that human sin dishonoured God and that only a God-man could render the satisfaction owed. It became the classic Western statement of satisfaction theory of the atonement.
events/anselm-cur-deus-homo-1098/consequ: Satisfaction theory and later penal substitution
events/bernard-founds-clairvaux-1115/sum: Bernard led twelve monks from Cîteaux to found Clairvaux, which became the dynamo of the Cistercian order's austere reform. Bernard became the most influential churchman of his age, preaching the Second Crusade and opposing Abelard.
events/bernard-founds-clairvaux-1115/con: Over 300 Cistercian houses by Bernard's death
events/second-lateran-council-1139/summa: Under Innocent II, the council declares marriages contracted by priests, deacons, subdeacons and professed religious to be invalid (canons 6–7), turning the long Gregorian campaign for clerical celibacy into an impediment to marriage in the Latin Church.
events/second-lateran-council-1139/cause: Concerns over church property and simony
events/abelard-condemned-1141/summary: At Bernard of Clairvaux's instigation, a council at Sens condemned propositions from Peter Abelard's teaching, including his account of the atonement as an example of love. Abelard retired to Cluny under Peter the Venerable and died in 1142.
events/abelard-condemned-1141/causes/0: Clash of dialectical theology and monastic theology
events/abelard-condemned-1141/consequenc: Moral influence theory recalled in modern theology
events/waldo-poor-of-lyon-1173/title: Peter Waldo and the Poor of Lyon
events/waldo-poor-of-lyon-1173/summary: The Lyon merchant Valdes (Peter Waldo) gave away his wealth, had the Gospels translated into the vernacular and began lay preaching. Condemned in 1184 for preaching without licence, the Waldensians survived persecution in Alpine valleys and joined the Reformed movement in 1532.
events/lalibela-rock-churches-1181/summa: King Gebre Meskel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty is credited with carving eleven monolithic churches from the rock at Roha, conceived as a 'New Jerusalem' after Saladin's capture of Jerusalem (1187) made pilgrimage difficult. They remain active places of Ethiopian Orthodox worship and pilgrimage.
events/sack-of-constantinople-1204/summa: Diverted by Venetian debts and a Byzantine succession dispute, crusaders stormed Constantinople in April 1204, looting churches and installing a Latin emperor and patriarch. Innocent III condemned the violence but accepted the Latin church. The Orthodox remembered the sack as the decisive betrayal that made the schism popular.
events/sack-of-constantinople-1204/longT: The Fourth Crusade was meant for Egypt. Unable to pay Venice for its fleet, the crusaders first attacked the Christian city of Zara and then agreed to restore the deposed Byzantine prince Alexios IV in exchange for money and the submission of the Greek church to Rome. When Alexios was murdered and payments failed, the crusaders sacked the city for three days, despoiling Hagia Sophia, where a prostitute was said to have been seated on the patriarchal throne. Relics, including the famous bronze horses now in Venice, were carried west. A Latin Empire ruled until 1261, and Greek bishops were replaced by Latins. For Orthodox Christians, 1204 transformed a clerical quarrel into a lived national grievance, explaining later resistance to the union of Florence. In 2001 Pope John Paul II expressed sorrow for the sack, and in 2004 he apologised to Patriarch Bartholomew.
events/sack-of-constantinople-1204/conse: Lasting Orthodox distrust of the West
Weakening of Byzantium before the Ottomans
events/albigensian-crusade-1209/summary: Innocent III launched a crusade against the dualist Cathars of Languedoc and their noble protectors. The massacre at Béziers in 1209 began two decades of war; the papal Inquisition was created afterward to root out remaining heresy.
events/albigensian-crusade-1209/conseque: Northern French control of the south
events/franciscan-order-1209/title: Francis of Assisi and the Friars Minor
events/franciscan-order-1209/summary: Francis, a merchant's son who embraced radical poverty, received oral approval of his simple rule from Innocent III in 1209. The Friars Minor spread rapidly through preaching and service; Francis went to Egypt during the Fifth Crusade (1219) to preach before Sultan al-Kamil.
events/franciscan-order-1209/causes/0: Urban wealth and lay religious hunger
events/franciscan-order-1209/consequence: Franciscan missions to Muslims and Mongols
events/fourth-lateran-council-1215/summa: Innocent III's great council of over 400 bishops defined that in the Eucharist the bread and wine are 'transubstantiated' into Christ's body and blood, required annual confession and communion, condemned Cathars, regulated clergy and imposed distinctive dress on Jews and Muslims. It marked the height of papal monarchy.
events/fourth-lateran-council-1215/longT: Fourth Lateran was the most important Western council of the Middle Ages. Its first constitution, a creed directed against Cathar dualism, contains the first conciliar use of 'transubstantiation'. Canon 21 (Omnis utriusque sexus) obliged every adult to confess to their own priest and receive communion at least at Easter, shaping lay piety for centuries. Other canons forbade new religious orders without approved rules, prohibited clergy from participating in ordeals, condemned Joachim of Fiore's Trinitarian views and planned a new crusade. Canon 68 required Jews and Muslims to wear distinguishing dress, contributing to later segregation. The council was attended by representatives of the Latin patriarchates set up after 1204. Protestant Reformers later rejected transubstantiation and compulsory auricular confession; Orthodox theology affirms the Eucharistic change but has generally avoided Aristotelian terminology.
events/dominican-order-1216/summary: Dominic de Guzmán, after preaching among Cathars in Languedoc, founded the Order of Preachers at Toulouse, approved by Honorius III in 1216. Committed to study and preaching, Dominicans dominated universities and later staffed the Inquisition.
events/dominican-order-1216/causes/0: Need for educated preachers against heresy
events/dominican-order-1216/consequences: Missions in the Americas and Asia
events/serbian-autocephaly-1219/summary: Sava, a Serbian prince turned Athonite monk, obtained from the patriarch at Nicaea recognition of an autocephalous Serbian archbishopric, based at Žiča. He organised dioceses and law, becoming Serbia's patron saint.
events/rubruck-at-karakorum-1254/title: William of Rubruck debates at Karakorum
events/rubruck-at-karakorum-1254/summary: The Flemish Franciscan William of Rubruck visited the Great Khan Möngke and took part in a formal religious debate among Latin Christians, Church of the East clergy, Muslims and Buddhists. His report describes a vigorous East Syriac Christianity at the Mongol court.
events/rubruck-at-karakorum-1254/causes/: Hopes of a Mongol alliance against Islam
events/mongol-sack-of-baghdad-1258/summa: Hülegü's Mongols destroyed the Abbasid caliphate; at the intervention of his Christian wife Doquz Khatun, Christians were largely spared and the catholicos received a palace. For a generation the Ilkhanate favoured Christians, before its rulers embraced Islam in 1295.
events/mongol-sack-of-baghdad-1258/conse: Brief golden age for Middle Eastern Christians
Backlash after the Ilkhans converted to Islam
events/aquinas-summa-1265/title: Thomas Aquinas begins the Summa Theologiae
events/aquinas-summa-1265/summary: Aquinas, Dominican master at Paris and in Italy, began the unfinished Summa Theologiae, synthesising Aristotle, Augustine and the Fathers in a structured account of God, creation, ethics and Christ. Declared the church's common doctor, his thought dominated Catholic theology after Trent and especially after 1879.
events/aquinas-summa-1265/causes/0: Recovery of Aristotle via Arabic and Greek sources
events/council-of-lyon-1274/summary: Gregory X's council received the submission of Byzantine envoys of Michael VIII, who accepted the Filioque and papal primacy to secure Western support. Bonaventure died during the council and Aquinas on his way to it. The union was repudiated by the Byzantine clergy and people and lapsed by 1282.
events/council-of-lyon-1274/longText: Michael VIII Palaiologos, who had recovered Constantinople in 1261, feared an attack by Charles of Anjou and sought papal protection through church union. At Lyon his envoys professed the Roman faith, including the procession of the Holy Spirit from Father and Son 'as from one principle', and the Greek and Latin creeds were sung. The council also reformed papal elections (the conclave) and approved new orders. In Byzantium the union was imposed by force against fierce monastic opposition, and after Michael's death in 1282 a synod repudiated it. Lyon became for the Orthodox a warning of union imposed for political ends; for Catholics a council counted as ecumenical.
events/council-of-lyon-1274/causes/0: Michael VIII's need for Western protection
events/council-of-lyon-1274/consequences: Definition of the Filioque 'as from one principle'
events/paris-condemnations-1277/summary: On 7 March 1277 Bishop Étienne Tempier of Paris condemned 219 philosophical and theological propositions associated with radical Aristotelians in the arts faculty — among them the eternity of the world and limits on God’s power — and touching some theses of Thomas Aquinas.
events/paris-condemnations-1277/causes/0: Spread of Aristotelian and Averroist natural philosophy at Paris
events/paris-condemnations-1277/causes/1: Spread of Aristotle and Averroes in the Paris Arts Faculty
events/paris-condemnations-1277/causes/2: Fears of a "double truth" and of limits placed on divine omnipotence
events/paris-condemnations-1277/conseque: Reasserted God’s absolute power and creation in time
Some historians (Duhem) see it as freeing natural philosophy from Aristotle; others dispute this
Strengthened emphasis on God’s absolute power, feeding Scotism and nominalism
Temporarily clouded Aquinas’s reputation until his canonisation in 1323
